title: 11 Reasons Why You Should Never, Ever Lose Your Cool e-your-cool/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin builds an extended argument, through eleven distinct reasons, against ever raising your voice or losing composure with students. He explains that losing one's cool sabotages rapport, weakens the leverage of a classroom management plan, undermines genuine accountability by shifting blame onto the teacher, and produces only temporary behavior improvement while worsening behavior—especially sneaky misbehavior—over time. Additional reasons include damaged parent relationships, eroded trust, a public admission of weak classroom management skills, a tense classroom atmosphere, modeling poor emotional regulation for students, and the personal toll of chronic stress that follows teachers home. Each reason is explained with a short paragraph of causal reasoning rather than just asserted. The piece closes by pointing to a calm, plan-based response to misbehavior as the antidote, framing composure as what allows a teacher to become the inspirational figure students remember.
points: Losing composure with students sabotages rapport built over weeks or months in an instant.
An emotional reaction to misbehavior undermines true accountability by giving students grounds to blame the teacher instead of reflecting.
Yelling produces only temporary improvement and tends to worsen behavior, especially sneaky misbehavior, over the long run.
Losing your cool is one of the most common sources of parent complaints and is difficult to defend.
Emotional outbursts model poor self-regulation, teaching students to fall apart when things don't go their way.
quotes: When you lose your cool you risk undoing weeks, or even months, of fruitful rapport-building with your students.
When you react emotionally to misbehavior you undermine true accountability—because it causes students to blame you, direct their simmering anger at you, and justify for their misbehavior.
Yelling, scolding and the like can result in immediate improvement. But alas, it’s only temporary.
Yelling at students is among the most common complaints from parents—and it’s difficult to defend.
When you bark at your students you’re announcing to them, your principal, other teachers, and everyone else within earshot that you don’t have effective classroom management skills.
Every time you lose your cool you provide a model—and your permission—for your students to do the same.
Yelling and scolding is incredibly stressful—and not just in the moment.
